ECE 343 Widget Bench

Interactive widgets for the ECE 343 companion app. Change any value and the plot redraws. Lossless lines unless a widget says otherwise; load sits at $z=0$ and the source at $z=-\ell$, as in class.

Standing waves

Incident and reflected waves add to a standing wave. Watch where the peaks and nulls sit as you change the load.

incidentreflectedtotal$|V(z)|$, in units of $|V_0^+|$
$$\Gamma_L=\frac{Z_L-Z_0}{Z_L+Z_0}$$$$\mathrm{VSWR}=\frac{1+|\Gamma_L|}{1-|\Gamma_L|}$$$$V(z)=V_0^+\left(e^{-j\beta z}+\Gamma_Le^{j\beta z}\right)$$

Line calculator

A generator driving a load through a lossless line. Every quantity from the course equation sheet, plus voltage and current along the line.

$|V(z)|$ (V)$|I(z)|\,Z_0$ (V)
$$Z_{\mathrm{in}}=Z_0\,\frac{Z_L+jZ_0\tan\beta\ell}{Z_0+jZ_L\tan\beta\ell}$$$$V_{\mathrm{in}}=V_s\,\frac{Z_{\mathrm{in}}}{Z_s+Z_{\mathrm{in}}}$$$$V_0^+=\frac{V_{\mathrm{in}}}{e^{j\beta\ell}+\Gamma_Le^{-j\beta\ell}}$$$$P_{\mathrm{av}}=\frac{|V_0^+|^2}{2Z_0}\left(1-|\Gamma_L|^2\right)$$

Smith chart

Tap or drag on the chart to place a load, then slide along the line toward the generator. The point rotates clockwise on its VSWR circle, one full turn per half wavelength.

load $z_L$path toward generator$z_{\mathrm{in}}$ at $d$$y_{\mathrm{in}}$ at $d$VSWR circle
$$z=\frac{Z}{Z_0}=\frac{1+\Gamma}{1-\Gamma}$$$$\Gamma(d)=\Gamma_Le^{-j2\beta d}$$$$y=\frac{1}{z}$$

Single-stub matching

A shunt stub at distance $d$ from the load. Move along the line until the admittance lands on the $g=1$ circle, then let the stub cancel the susceptance.

load $y_L$line of length $d$$y(d)=1+jb$stub adds $-jb$$g=1$ circle
$$\text{shorted: } y_{\mathrm{stub}}=-j\cot\beta\ell_s$$$$\text{open: } y_{\mathrm{stub}}=+j\tan\beta\ell_s$$$$\text{need: } y_{\mathrm{stub}}=-jb$$

Line parameters

From geometry or $R'$, $L'$, $G'$, $C'$ to propagation constant and characteristic impedance. A lossy line shows its exponential decay below.

$\mathbf{E}$ (radial)$\mathbf{H}$ (circles)

Phasor rotator

A phasor is a complex number that spins at $\omega$. Its shadow on the real axis is the cosine you see in time. Add a second phasor at the same frequency and the sum spins with them.

$\tilde V_1e^{j\omega t}$$\tilde V_2e^{j\omega t}$sumreal part $v(t)$
$v_1(t)$$v_2(t)$$v_1+v_2$
$$v(t)=\mathrm{Re}\left\{\tilde Ve^{j\omega t}\right\}$$$$A\cos(\omega t+\phi)\ \leftrightarrow\ Ae^{j\phi}$$$$e^{j\theta}=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta$$$$\frac{d}{dt}\ \leftrightarrow\ j\omega$$

Traveling wave

A sinusoid in space and time. Follow the marked crest: it moves one wavelength every period, at the phase velocity. Raise $\varepsilon_r$ and the wave slows down and gets shorter.

$E(z,t)$ nowat $t=0$envelope $e^{\mp\alpha z}$one crest
$$E(z,t)=E_0e^{-\alpha z}\cos(\omega t-\beta z)$$$$u_p=\frac{\omega}{\beta}=\frac{c}{\sqrt{\mu_r\varepsilon_r}}$$$$\lambda=\frac{u_p}{f}=\frac{2\pi}{\beta}$$

Coordinate explorer

One point, three coordinate systems. Enter it in any system, then look at the unit vectors there. Cylindrical and spherical unit vectors change direction from point to point. Drag the picture sideways to turn it.

point $P$1st unit vector2nd3rd
$$r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2},\quad \phi=\tan^{-1}\frac{y}{x}$$$$R=\sqrt{r^2+z^2},\quad \theta=\cos^{-1}\frac{z}{R}$$$$d\mathbf{l}=\hat{\mathbf{r}}\,dr+\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}\,r\,d\phi+\hat{\mathbf{z}}\,dz$$$$dV=R^2\sin\theta\,dR\,d\theta\,d\phi$$

Divergence and curl

Pick a field. The shading shows divergence (sources and sinks) or curl (swirl). Tap the plot to move the probe. Arrows leaving its box more than entering mean positive divergence, and its paddle wheel spins at a rate set by the curl.

positivenegativeprobe
$$\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}=\frac{\partial F_x}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial F_y}{\partial y}$$$$(\nabla\times\mathbf{F})_z=\frac{\partial F_y}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial F_x}{\partial y}$$

Point charges

Field lines and equipotentials for up to three point charges. Drag a charge to move it; tap anywhere else to move the probe and read $\mathbf{E}$ and $V$ there.

field line$V>0$$V<0$probe
$$\mathbf{E}=\sum_i\frac{Q_i}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{R}_i}{|\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{R}_i|^3}$$$$V=\sum_i\frac{Q_i}{4\pi\varepsilon_0|\mathbf{R}-\mathbf{R}_i|}$$$$\mathbf{E}=-\nabla V$$

Gauss's law

Grow the Gaussian surface and watch the enclosed charge. With enough symmetry, $D$ is the same everywhere on the surface, so the flux is just $D$ times the area.

chargeGaussian surface$\mathbf{D}$ through the surface
$E$at the surface
$$\oint_S\mathbf{D}\cdot d\mathbf{s}=Q_{\mathrm{enc}}$$$$\text{sphere: }D_R\,4\pi R^2=Q_{\mathrm{enc}}$$$$\text{cylinder: }D_r\,2\pi r\ell=\rho_l\ell$$

Dielectric boundary

A field crosses from medium 1 into medium 2. Tangential $\mathbf{E}$ carries straight over; normal $\mathbf{D}$ carries over too unless there is surface charge. So the field bends at the interface.

$\mathbf{E}_1$$\mathbf{E}_2$tangential and normal parts
$$E_{1t}=E_{2t}$$$$\varepsilon_1E_{1n}-\varepsilon_2E_{2n}=\rho_s$$$$\frac{\tan\theta_1}{\tan\theta_2}=\frac{\varepsilon_1}{\varepsilon_2}\quad(\rho_s=0)$$

Capacitor builder

Choose a geometry and size it. The plot shows the field and potential between the conductors; the readouts give $C$, the stored energy, and the voltage where the dielectric would break down.

$E$$V$
$$C_{\text{plate}}=\frac{\varepsilon A}{d}$$$$C'_{\text{coax}}=\frac{2\pi\varepsilon}{\ln(b/a)}$$$$C_{\text{sphere}}=\frac{4\pi\varepsilon ab}{b-a}$$$$W_e=\tfrac12CV^2$$

Conductor and resistance

Push a current through a round wire. The field inside is tiny for a good conductor, and the electrons drift backward against it far more slowly than you might expect.

$\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{J}$electrons (drift shown sped up)
$$R=\frac{\ell}{\sigma A}$$$$\mathbf{J}=\sigma\mathbf{E}$$$$\mathbf{J}=\rho_v\mathbf{u}$$$$P=I^2R$$

Biot–Savart builder

Every bit of current $I\,d\mathbf{l}$ adds a little $d\mathbf{H}$ at the field point. The dots on the source show how much each piece contributes; nearby pieces count most.

currentsize of each piece's $dH$$d\mathbf{H}$ and total $\mathbf{H}$
$H$referencefield point
$$d\mathbf{H}=\frac{I}{4\pi}\frac{d\mathbf{l}\times\hat{\mathbf{R}}}{R^2}$$$$H_{\text{segment}}=\frac{I}{4\pi r}(\cos\alpha_1-\cos\alpha_2)$$$$H_{\text{loop axis}}=\frac{Ia^2}{2(a^2+z^2)^{3/2}}$$

Ampère's law

Grow the Amperian loop and count the current through it. With circular symmetry, $H$ is the same all the way around, so $H$ times the circumference equals the enclosed current.

current out of the pageinto the pageAmperian loop$\mathbf{H}$
$H(r)$at the loop
$$\oint_C\mathbf{H}\cdot d\mathbf{l}=I_{\mathrm{enc}}$$$$H\,(2\pi r)=I_{\mathrm{enc}}$$$$\mathbf{B}=\mu\mathbf{H}$$

Magnetic boundary

$\mathbf{B}$ crosses from medium 1 into medium 2. Normal $\mathbf{B}$ carries over; tangential $\mathbf{H}$ carries over unless a surface current flows. Try iron ($\mu_r=1000$) against air.

$\mathbf{B}_1$$\mathbf{B}_2$tangential and normal parts
$$B_{1n}=B_{2n}$$$$\hat{\mathbf{n}}_2\times(\mathbf{H}_1-\mathbf{H}_2)=\mathbf{J}_s$$$$\frac{\tan\theta_1}{\tan\theta_2}=\frac{\mu_1}{\mu_2}\quad(J_s=0)$$

Faraday and Lenz

Change the flux through a loop and an EMF appears. The induced current (arrows on the loop) always pushes back against the change. Watch the EMF peak where the flux changes fastest, not where it is largest.

$\mathbf{B}$induced current
flux linkage $N\Phi$EMFnow
$$V_{\mathrm{emf}}=-N\frac{d\Phi}{dt}$$$$V_{\text{bar}}=uB\ell$$$$V_{\text{gen}}=NBA\omega\sin\omega t$$

Conduction versus displacement current

A sinusoidal field drives two currents in a material: conduction $\sigma E$, flat with frequency, and displacement $\omega\varepsilon E$, rising with frequency. Where they cross, the material changes from conductor-like to dielectric-like.

conduction $\sigma$displacement $\omega\varepsilon$chosen frequency
$$\nabla\times\mathbf{H}=\sigma\mathbf{E}+j\omega\varepsilon\mathbf{E}$$$$\frac{|J_c|}{|J_d|}=\frac{\sigma}{\omega\varepsilon}$$$$\tau_r=\frac{\varepsilon}{\sigma}$$

Plane wave in a medium

$\mathbf{E}$ (along $x$) and $\mathbf{H}$ (along $y$) travel together toward $+z$. Pick a material and frequency: in a lossy medium the wave shrinks as $e^{-\alpha z}$ and $\mathbf{H}$ lags $\mathbf{E}$ by the angle of $\eta_c$.

$\mathbf{E}$ along $x$$\mathbf{H}$ along $y$ (scaled to $E$)envelope $e^{-\alpha z}$
$$\gamma=\alpha+j\beta=j\omega\sqrt{\mu\left(\varepsilon-j\frac{\sigma}{\omega}\right)}$$$$\eta_c=\sqrt{\frac{j\omega\mu}{\sigma+j\omega\varepsilon}}$$$$S_{\mathrm{av}}=\frac{|E_0|^2}{2|\eta_c|}e^{-2\alpha z}\cos\theta_\eta$$

Skin depth

At high frequency, current in a conductor crowds into a thin layer at the surface. The field and current fall as $e^{-d/\delta_s}$ with depth $d$, and $\delta_s$ shrinks as $1/\sqrt{f}$. The wire cross-section shows where the current flows.

current density, stronger colour is denserone skin depth in from the surface
$|J|/|J_0|=e^{-d/\delta_s}$$d=\delta_s,2\delta_s,\dots$
$$\delta_s=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi f\mu\sigma}}$$$$R_s=\frac{1}{\sigma\delta_s}$$$$\frac{R_{\mathrm{ac}}}{R_{\mathrm{dc}}}\approx\frac{a}{2\delta_s}\quad(\delta_s\ll a)$$

Polarization ellipse

Two perpendicular components, $a_x$ and $a_y$, with a phase difference $\delta$. Their sum traces a line, a circle or an ellipse. The top view looks back at the wave as it comes toward you; the bottom view freezes time and shows $\mathbf{E}$ along $z$.

$\mathbf{E}$ now$E_x$, $E_y$ellipse tracedmajor axis at $\gamma$
$$\tilde{\mathbf{E}}=(\hat{\mathbf{x}}a_x+\hat{\mathbf{y}}a_ye^{j\delta})e^{-jkz}$$$$\tan2\gamma=\tan2\psi_0\cos\delta$$$$\sin2\chi=\sin2\psi_0\sin\delta$$$$R=\frac{1}{|\tan\chi|}$$
